title: 41. The Event Object
theory:
When an event occurs (like a mouse click or a key press), the browser automatically gathers detailed information about that event—such as the exact X and Y coordinates of the mouse, or which specific key was pressed. It packages all this data into an Event Object.

If you put a parameter (usually named e or event) inside your event listener function, JavaScript will automatically pass this Event Object into your function when the event triggers.

This is incredibly useful! For example, in a game, you need to know exactly which key the user pressed to move the character.

title: 42. Asynchronous JavaScript Introduction
theory:
JavaScript is a Single-Threaded language, meaning it can only execute one line of code at a time on a single main thread. If a piece of code takes 5 seconds to run (like downloading a large image), the entire webpage would freeze for 5 seconds!

The Solution: Asynchronous Programming

To prevent the browser from freezing, JavaScript offloads heavy tasks (like timers or fetching data from a server) to the browser's Web APIs. The browser handles the heavy lifting in the background, and when it finishes, it alerts JavaScript to execute a callback function.

This allows JavaScript to continue running other code smoothly while waiting for background tasks to finish.
output:
> 1. Starting task...
> 3. Other code runs immediately!
> 2. Data downloaded! (after 2 seconds)

title: 43. The Problem: Callback Hell
theory:
When dealing with Asynchronous code, we use "Callback" functions to tell the program what to do once the data is ready. But what happens if you need to fetch Data A, then use Data A to fetch Data B, and then use Data B to fetch Data C?

You end up nesting callback functions inside callback functions inside callback functions. This creates a massive, horizontal, triangle-shaped block of code known in the industry as Callback Hell or the Pyramid of Doom.

It makes the code incredibly hard to read, scale, and debug. To solve this, JavaScript introduced Promises.
output:
> User downloaded.
> Posts downloaded.
> Comments downloaded.
> Finished.

title: 44. Introduction to Promises
theory:
A Promise is an object representing the eventual completion (or failure) of an asynchronous operation. Think of it like a restaurant buzzer: you place your order, and they hand you a buzzer. The buzzer is a "promise" that you will eventually get your food.

The 3 States of a Promise:

  1. Pending: The initial state. The background task is still running. (You are waiting for the food).
  2. Fulfilled (Resolved): The task completed successfully! (The buzzer rings, your food is ready).
  3. Rejected: The task failed due to an error. (The kitchen ran out of ingredients).
output:
> Promise is pending...
> (after 2 seconds)
> Data successfully fetched!

title: 45. Consuming Promises (.then & .catch)
theory:
Once you have a Promise (like the one returned by an API call), you need to handle what happens when it resolves or rejects. We "consume" promises using two chained methods.

.then()

This block of code executes ONLY if the Promise resolves successfully. The data passed into the resolve() function is sent here.

.catch()

This block of code executes ONLY if the Promise is rejected (e.g., the Wi-Fi dropped). This allows you to handle errors gracefully without crashing the app.
output:
> Waiting for data...
> Success! Data successfully fetched!

title: 46. Async and Await (Modern JS)
theory:
While .then() and .catch() solved Callback Hell, chaining them could still look messy. In 2017, JavaScript introduced Async / Await, which is syntactic sugar over Promises.

It allows us to write asynchronous code that looks and behaves like synchronous, line-by-line code!

How it works:

  • Put the async keyword in front of a function to declare it as asynchronous.
  • Inside that function, use the await keyword in front of any Promise.
  • The function will literally pause execution at the await line until the Promise resolves, and then store the result in a variable.
output:
> Logging in...
> User profile loaded: Admin

title: 47. Handling Errors with try/catch
theory:
When using Async/Await, we no longer use .catch(). Instead, we use standard try/catch blocks, which is how error handling is done in traditional languages like Java or Python.

You put the risky code (like fetching data from a server) inside the try block. If any Promise is rejected, JavaScript immediately stops the try block and jumps straight into the catch block, passing the error along.

This makes handling errors extremely clean and predictable.
output:
> Starting data fetch...
> An error occurred: Server is down!
> Execution continues normally.

title: 48. The Fetch API
theory:
The Fetch API is a modern, built-in browser tool used to make HTTP network requests (like pulling data from a database or a third-party server). It completely replaces the older, clunky XMLHttpRequest.

fetch() requires a URL and automatically returns a Promise. When the server responds, the Promise resolves into a Response object.

The JSON Step

The raw response is not immediately usable in JavaScript. You must call response.json() to convert the incoming data packet into a native JavaScript Object. Note that .json() also returns a Promise, so you must await it twice!
output:
> Fetching User Data...
> User Name: Leanne Graham
> Email: Sincere@april.biz

title: 49. Introduction to Object-Oriented JS
theory:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming paradigm based on the concept of "objects", which can contain data and code to manipulate that data.

Instead of writing 100 loose variables and functions, OOP allows you to bundle related variables and functions into a single logical entity. For example, a BankAccount object would hold the `balance` (data) and the `deposit()` function (behavior).

Classes (The Blueprint)

A Class is a blueprint or template for creating objects. You define the structure in the Class, and then you "instantiate" (create) multiple individual objects based on that blueprint.
output:
> New account created for Alice
> Balance: 0
> New account created for Bob
> Balance: 0

title: 50. OOP Methods and Encapsulation
theory:
Once we have a Class, we want to add behaviors to it. We do this by defining Methods inside the Class block.

In a properly designed OOP system, outside code shouldn't manually change the internal data (like account.balance = 5000). Instead, the outside code should call methods (like account.deposit(5000)), and the object updates its own internal data.

This concept of hiding internal state and requiring interaction through defined methods is called Encapsulation. It prevents bugs and makes code highly predictable.
output:
> Deposited: 100
> Current Balance: 100
> Withdrew: 40
> Current Balance: 60
